# Roadwright

Draw a shape. See the road it rolls on.

Live at https://baselashraf.com/roadwright/
Source at https://github.com/BaselAshraf81/roadwright

## What it does

You draw a closed shape. Roadwright works out the road profile that shape rolls
along while its axle stays at a constant height, then animates it rolling. A square
rolls on a row of inverted catenaries. A pentagon, a star, or a hand-drawn blob each
roll on something different.

## The mathematics

Describe the wheel in polar form as r(theta) measured from its axle. For the axle to
travel level, the contact point sits directly below it at distance r, so the road
height is y = -r. Rolling without slipping matches arc length along the road to arc
length along the wheel, which gives dx = r dtheta. Therefore:

  x(theta) = integral of r dtheta
  y(theta) = -r(theta)

Read backwards, road to wheel:

  theta(x) = integral of dx / (-y(x))
  r(theta) = -y(x(theta))

Both directions are quadratures. There is no solver, no iteration, and no
convergence tolerance, which is why the road can be recomputed while a control is
being dragged.

A periodic road carries a closed wheel only when the total angle turned over one
period is exactly one full turn: integral of dx / (-y) = 2*pi.

## What is verified, by automated test

- A square wheel of half-side a returns y = -a*cosh(x/a), an inverted catenary, to
  better than one part in a million.
- A circle returns a flat road.
- Road arc length equals the wheel perimeter, which is what rolling without slipping
  means.
- The road's horizontal period is NOT the wheel perimeter. For a square of half-side
  a it is 8*a*ln(1 + sqrt(2)), about 7.0509a, against a perimeter of 8a. Only a
  circle makes the two quantities agree.
- Wheel to road to wheel round-trips, so both directions agree.
- Interference, meaning how far a wheel drives into its own road, is measured rather
  than estimated. A circle and a square measure zero. An equilateral triangle
  measures 4.7 percent and a five-pointed star 21.5 percent, and neither can be
  built, which matches the known fact that a rolling equilateral triangle jams
  because its corners bind in the ruts.
- A wheelbase of a whole number of road periods puts two independent wheels in
  identical orientation, which follows from the closure condition.

## Constraints, stated honestly

- The wheel must be star-shaped about its axle, meaning a ray from the axle crosses
  the outline exactly once in every direction. Drawings that fail this are bridged
  into the closest shape that satisfies it, and the change is shown and reported
  rather than applied silently.
- A shape can be perfectly valid on paper and impossible to build. Sharp corners
  drive into the road as the wheel turns. The interference figure reports this.
- Tilting the road is exact rather than an approximation. The derivation never
  mentions gravity; it only requires the axle to travel along a straight line, and
  nothing requires that line to be horizontal.

## Sources

- Leon Hall and Stan Wagon, "Roads and Wheels", Mathematics Magazine 65 (1992).
- G. B. Robison derived the general road-wheel equations in 1960.
- Stan Wagon and Loren Kellen built a square-wheeled bicycle at Macalester College
  in 1997. The National Museum of Mathematics and the Exploratorium both exhibit a
  square-wheeled tricycle.
